To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cholinergic stimulation improves performance on a hippocampally mediated task.
nicotine improves performance on a hippocampus-dependent task of visual perception.
nicotine improves performance on a hippocampus-dependent attention task, and that this effect is predicted by how much someone smokes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms that underlie the control of attention and perception.
the role of the hippocampus in the control of attention.
the role of acetylcholine in attention and perception, and how this might be related to the hippocampus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
nicotine increases attention to spatial relationships in the hippocampus, but not to the relationship between visual features, as measured by performance on an attention task.
nicotine improves the hippocampus ability to discriminate spatial relationships between visual stimuli.
nicotine improves performance on the similar rooms task, and that the individual differences in expired breath CO levels predict the improvements in performance on the similar art task.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nicotine enhances the ability to perceive the relations between environmental features.
nicotine enhances hippocampally-mediated perception and attention, and this is mediated by the hippocampus' ability to process spatial relations.
the hippocampus has a unique ability to represent relations between visual features, which can be modulated by the cholinergic system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cholinergic drugs can enhance the ability to perceive spatial relations between objects.
nicotine enhances the ability of people to attend to the spatial relations in a scene.
nicotine can enhance the ability to detect spatial relations.
